However, the claim's characterization that AQAP was 'actively reduced' is contradicted by the source, which states the deals 'allowed al-Qaida militants to survive to fight another day — and risk strengthening' AQAP. The claim's 'without military intervention' is also imprecise, as the source notes 'The clearing of al-Qaida from Shabwa and other provinces did not completely take place without fighting.'
rows.source_quote: many of their conquests came without firing a shot. That's because the coalition cut secret deals with al-Qaida fighters, paying some to leave key cities and towns and letting others retreat with weapons, equipment and wads of looted cash ... Hundreds more were recruited to join the coalition itself. ... Coalition-backed militias actively recruit al-Qaida militants, or those who were recently members, because they're considered exceptional fighters, the AP found.

rows.comments: The source confirms the regiment's participation at Belmont (23rd November 1899), Modder River (28th November), and Magersfontein (11th December). However, the claim contains errors: (1) Relief of Kimberley occurred in February 1900, not 'winter 1899' — February is summer in South Africa; (2) the source states the brigade 'were not in the force which headed off Cronje on the 17th,' partially contradicting the claim that the regiment took part in Paardeberg resulting in Cronjé's surrender, though the Abadie entry does mention 'operations at Paardeberg (17 to 26 February).' The source does not explicitly state that Paardeberg 'resulted in Piet Cronjé's surrender.'
rows.source_quote: When the march to Kimberley commenced on 11th February the 9th and 16th formed the 3rd Cavalry Brigade under Brigadier General J R P Gordon. ... After Kimberley was relieved the brigade took part in the other operations antecedent to the occupation of Bloemfontein, but were not in the force which headed off Cronje on the 17th.

rows.comments: The source confirms the Olmsted Brothers proposed the loop as part of planning for the Lewis and Clark Centennial Exposition, that it has expanded to more than 140 miles, encircles the city, and connects parks along the Columbia, Sandy, and Willamette Rivers and Johnson Creek. The only minor discrepancy is the claim says '140 miles' while the source says 'more than 140 miles.' The source does not specify the year 1905 for the exposition, but does not contradict it either.
rows.source_quote: The 40-Mile Loop was originally proposed in 1904 by the Olmsted Brothers (Frederick Law, Jr. and John Charles, sons of Frederick Law Olmstead) who were brought to Portland from Boston to propose a park system as part of the planning for the Lewis and Clark Centennial Exposition and World's Fair. ... the planned loop trail has lengthened to more than 140 miles ... The trail connects parks along the Columbia, Sandy, and Willamette Rivers and Johnson Creek in an almost continuous loop.

rows.comments: The source supports that Fraske is considered the last veteran of the Indian Wars and confirms his birth year as 1872. However, the claim states his death date as June 18, 1973, while the source explicitly says June 8th, 1973 — a direct contradiction. The source also does not mention a middle initial 'W.' or the alternate spelling 'Fredrak,' nor a specific birth date of March 8.
rows.source_quote: Fraske died on June 8th, 1973, at the age 0f 101 and is widely considered to be the last veteran of the Indian Wars.
